Stage 3 · Grammar

Saying what you can and could do

One idea, three forms — and only one of them changes for time.

Read these four sentences from the lesson.
  • The human brain can think creatively.
  • Computers aren’t able to feel emotions.
  • Ten years ago you couldn’t understand this sentence.
  • We will be able to talk to robots in the future.
Look at the four sentences. What comes after can, could and be able to?
The three forms
TimePositiveNegativeQuestionShort answer
now · canShe can read a map.She can’t read a map.Can she read a map?Yes, she can. / No, she can’t.
now · be able toShe is able to read a map.She isn’t able to read a map.Is she able to read a map?Yes, she is. / No, she isn’t.
past · couldI could swim at five.I couldn’t swim at five.Could you swim at five?Yes, I could. / No, I couldn’t.
past · was/were able toI was able to swim at five.I wasn’t able to swim at five.Were you able to swim?Yes, I was. / No, I wasn’t.
futureShe will be able to read a map.  —  there is no future of can, so be able to fills the gap. Not will can.
after another verbI’d like to be able to drive. · She might be able to help.  —  again can cannot go there.
one past successThe fire started, but everyone was able to get out.  Not could get out — for one thing that really happened once, use was/were able to.
the ability word the plain verb

FORM. can / can’t / could / couldn’t + the plain verb. be able to + to + the plain verb. Never can to, never can swimming.

USE. can = ability now · could = ability over a period in the past · be able to = the same idea in the tenses can does not have (future, present perfect, after another verb).

Not “I will can help”, not “I can to drive”, not “She cans read”.

Obligation — must and have to — comes next lesson, and it behaves the same way after the modal.

FORM. can and could are modal verbs. They never add -s, they never take to after them, and the verb behind them stays plain: she can read, he could swim. be able to is different: it is the verb be plus able to, so it changes like any other verb — am / is / are / was / were / will be / have been able to.

USE. Use can for ability now and could for ability that lasted over a period in the past: I could read before I started school. Use be able to when can has no form to give you — the future (I will be able to), after another verb (I want to be able to), and after have (I have never been able to).

The one exception worth knowing. For a single thing that really happened once in the past, English prefers was/were able to, not could: The lift stopped, but we were able to open the doors. With see, hear, understand, remember, could is normal even for one moment: I could hear music.

Three mistakes to watch: “I will can help you” (no future of can) · “She can to drive” (no to after a modal) · “He cans swim” (modals never take -s).

Next lesson the same pattern comes back with obligation: must behaves like can, and have to behaves like be able to.

Real sentences from the coursebook grammar recording.

Full grammar reference — can, could and be able to

Form

Ability nowI can swim. · She can’t drive. · Can you cook?
Ability in the pastI could read at four. · He couldn’t come.
Other tensesI’ve never been able to remember names. · You’ll be able to read this soon.
Short answersYes, I can. / No, I can’t. · Yes, I could.
Form rulecan and could take the plain verb; be able to takes to + verb.

Spelling and sound

cannot is written as one word; the short form is can’t.

When and why we use it

  • Can and could have no infinitive and no -ing, so be able to fills the gaps: after will, have, to and -ing.
  • Could describes a general ability in the past. For one successful occasion, use was able to or managed to: The door was locked, but I managed to open it.
  • Can is also used for permission and for requests: Can I sit here?
  • Could softens a request in the present: Could you repeat that?

Signal words

at all · quite well · not very well · never · when I was young

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I can to swim. → I can swim.No to after can.
  • She cans drive. → She can drive.Modals never take -s.
  • I will can come. → I will be able to come.Two modals cannot stand together.
  • I have never could do it. → I have never been able to do it.Could has no participle.

Don’t confuse it with

could = a general past ability. was able to = you succeeded on one particular occasion.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

What the brain really does, and what people only think it does.

Before you read: many people say we use only ten per cent of the brain.

Do you think that is true? Decide first, then read and find out if you were right.

There is no right answer yet. This is your prediction.

What the brain can really do

People love stories about the brain. One of them says that we use only ten per cent of it. It is a myth. Scientists can now watch the brain at work, and nobody has ever found a silent ninety per cent. The brain is about two per cent of your body, but it takes about twenty per cent of your energy.

Other myths are just as popular. In the 1990s many people believed that classical music could make a child more intelligent. Researchers checked it carefully. Music can put you in a better mood, and a good mood helps you solve problems — but Mozart cannot give a child a talent it did not have.

So what is really true? In 2000 a team in London studied taxi drivers. To get their licence, the drivers had to learn every street in the city. The part of the brain we use for map reading was larger in the drivers than in other people, and the longer they had driven, the larger it was. They were not born with this ability. They built it.

That is the interesting part. Ten years ago you could not understand this sentence. Now you can read it. Nothing changed in your head by accident: you practised, and the connections grew.

The brain can also do something no machine can: it can imagine a place it has never seen. Computers are still not able to copy that — and they are not able to feel emotions either.

Your brain will not be able to give you a perfect memory: it cannot remember everything you read, and it never could. But almost everyone can achieve something new — a language, an instrument, a different job — at almost any age.

Sources. Ten-per-cent myth and brain energy use: Society for Neuroscience, Brain Facts; Raichle & Gusnard (2002), PNAS · Mozart effect: Pietschnig, Voracek & Formann (2010), Intelligence · London taxi drivers: Maguire et al. (2000), PNAS. Text written for this course.
